set.statement: In people who use opioids, a period without them is thought to lower tolerance, so that an amount that was once usual may have a much greater effect, including on breathing, when use starts again. One small follow-up study after inpatient detoxification, the only primary study of this read, fits that idea but did not measure tolerance, and two narrative reviews give no estimate, so the evidence is insufficient to say how long a break must last, how fast tolerance falls, or by how much the chance of a fatal overdose rises. In London, 137 consecutive people dependent on opiates who went through detoxification within a 28-day inpatient programme, recruited over 20 months and followed for 12 months after discharge (vital status known for all), had three overdose deaths, all within four months of discharge and all among the 37 who completed both the detoxification and the whole programme (3 of 37, about 8 in 100, editors' calculation); none of the 57 who completed the detoxification but left the programme early, or of the 43 who did not complete it, died of an overdose (0 of 100). Two other people died of other causes after a relapse, one in each group that had completed the detoxification, and the authors' exact test across the three groups gave P = 0.02 without saying whether it compared all deaths or overdose deaths (Strang et al., 2003). The authors labelled the groups by the tolerance they presumed each had on leaving ('still tolerant', 'reduced tolerance', 'lost tolerance') and attribute the clustering to lost tolerance, but they measured neither tolerance nor drug use after discharge; the groups were defined by whether people finished treatment, which may go with other differences; and the five people who died, of any cause, differed from the other 132 in the month before admission: four had lived alone, against 21 of 130, and they had been prescribed higher methadone doses and had used heroin on fewer days. With three overdose deaths and no adjustment, chance and these differences cannot be ruled out; the authors call for replication. The idea itself is described second-hand by two narrative reviews. White and Irvine (1999) offer it as a possible explanation and rest it on one hair-analysis study (less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which they read as a sign of lower use before death); they say that information on the rate of loss is sparse and that the loss may be quick and uneven between effects, and they describe two studies in people on methadone maintenance that found tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone to be incomplete. Hickman et al. (2008) say, citing White and Irvine, that risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification; White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence, and separately of treatment with naltrexone, and do not name either of those settings. Deaths after release from prison, and after leaving methadone or buprenorphine treatment, are separate answers. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
set.plain: Does tolerance drop after a break from opioids? That's the usual explanation, and one small study fits it, but no study here measured tolerance, or how fast it falls. In London, 137 people who went through a 28-day hospital detox were followed for a year after leaving. Three died of an overdose, all within 4 months, and all 3 were among the 37 who finished both the detox and the whole programme; none of the 100 who left earlier died of an overdose. The researchers think the people who stayed to the end had lost their tolerance, but they never measured it, and with only 3 deaths, chance or other differences could explain the pattern: 4 of the 5 people who died, from any cause, had lived alone, against about 16 in 100 of the others. Two review articles offer the same explanation but give no numbers for how long a break has to be, how fast tolerance falls, or how much the risk goes up; the main study behind them was one on hair samples. Even people who have used opioids for a long time may keep some risk of slowed breathing, according to two studies of people on methadone described in one review.
set.population: People dependent on opiates leaving inpatient detoxification within a 28-day programme at one London unit (137 consecutive consenting admissions recruited over 20 months, followed for 12 months; Strang et al., 2003); and people who use opioids (heroin, methadone and other opioids) as described in two narrative reviews
set.exposure: A period without opioids before use starts again: in the follow-up study, completing both the detoxification and the whole inpatient programme (the group the authors presumed had lost tolerance; tolerance was not measured); in the reviews, a period of abstinence
set.comparator: In the follow-up study, people who completed the detoxification but left the programme early, or did not complete it (presumed by the authors to have reduced or kept their tolerance); in the reviews, continued regular use and the same person's tolerance before the break
set.outcome: Death from overdose, and from any cause, within 12 months of leaving inpatient detoxification; tolerance to opioid effects, including breathing depression (measured in none of the sources), and the chance of a fatal overdose when use starts again
set.magnitude: Strang et al. (2003), 137 people followed for 12 months after leaving a 28-day inpatient detoxification programme: overdose deaths 3 of 37 who completed detoxification and the programme (8.1%, exact 95% CI 1.7% to 21.9%, editors' calculation), 0 of 57 who completed detoxification but left early and 0 of 43 who did not complete it (0 of 100, 0% to 3.6%, editors' calculation); all three within 4 months of discharge. All deaths 4 of 37, 1 of 57 and 0 of 43 (Fisher's exact test, df = 2, P = 0.02; the text does not say whether all deaths or overdose deaths were tested; exact tests on the printed counts give 0.021 and 0.019, editors' calculation). The 5 who died against the other 132 (month before admission): lived alone 4 (80%) against 21 of 130 (16%), Fisher P = 0.004; prescribed methadone 51.0 mg (SD 20.7) against 29.2 mg (SD 23.1), P = 0.04; days of heroin use 14.4 (SD 14.4) against 24.5 (SD 10.2), P = 0.03; inpatient stay 24.6 against 15.6 days, P = 0.02; completed the programme 4 (80%) against 33 (25%), P = 0.02; twelve characteristics compared without correction. Authors' expectation from earlier data: one or two deaths within a year, one from overdose. No measure of tolerance. White and Irvine (1999), second-hand: one hair-analysis study (Tagliaro et al., 1998) found lower morphine content in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using (no numbers given in the review); the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is called sparse, probably uneven and possibly quick (receptor changes can occur in minutes or hours); incomplete tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone in two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago et al., 1977; no numbers given). Hickman et al. (2008): risk appears to be raised after periods of relative abstinence; no figures.

grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The follow-up study (card sc_strang_2003: ROBINS-I serious) could adjust for nothing with five deaths; the groups selected themselves by finishing treatment, the people who died differed in living alone, prescribed methadone dose and days of heroin use, and the source used to class a death as overdose is not stated. The primary studies behind the reviews (one hair-analysis study of people who died of overdose; two studies of people on methadone) cannot be appraised from the reviews.

grade.domains.inconsistency.note: No conflicting finding: the follow-up study and the reviews point the same way, although the 57 people the study presumed to have reduced tolerance had no overdose death, so its gradient rests on three deaths.

grade.domains.indirectness.note: Tolerance was never measured: finishing treatment stands in for it, so the claim's outcome (lost tolerance and the size of the risk when use starts again) is inferred. The reviews are second-hand, one citing the other, and the settings named (incarceration, detoxification) come from the later review only. The follow-up study is one London inpatient unit.

grade.domains.imprecision.note: Three overdose deaths: 3 of 37 (exact 95% CI 1.7% to 21.9%) against 0 of 100 (0% to 3.6%), editors' calculation; no estimate of the size of the risk is possible.

grade.domains.publication_bias.note: Not assessable; one small study with a positive result, whose authors call for replication.

set.grade.reasoning: The claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews: Strang et al. (2003), a prospective follow-up of 137 people after inpatient detoxification, is the first primary study read on it. Observational evidence starts low; down one level for risk of bias (no adjustment possible, self-selected groups, the people who died differing in other ways), one for indirectness (tolerance never measured; the reviews second-hand) and one for imprecision (three overdose deaths): very low, as in version 0.1.2, now for these reasons. The reviews supply the idea and the methadone breathing studies second-hand and do not raise the rating. Relation: insufficient evidence, because no source gives a time course, a size for the loss of tolerance or a size for the risk; the follow-up study shows where three deaths fell, not how much risk rises. The labels 'reduced' and 'lost tolerance' are the authors'; the statement describes the groups by what people did. Status: single study (one primary study read; the two reviews, one citing the other, describe other studies second-hand). Because a supporting anchor is now a primary study, the narrative-review rule (METHODS 6.3) no longer applies; the claim stays at draft until a round-2 reader has checked the new anchors.
set.verification.flag_note: Round pdf-2026-11-14: Strang et al. (2003) added as anchors 6 to 9 (ai-located by AI reader 685, claim writer, from the PDF); the claim no longer rests only on narrative reviews and can move up the ladder once a round-2 reader has checked them. Earlier notes kept: the examples of prison and detoxification are Hickman et al.'s addition; White and Irvine write only of a period of abstinence (their pp. 966-967) and of naltrexone treatment (p. 968). The primary studies named by White and Irvine (Tagliaro et al. 1998; Marks and Goldring 1973; Santiago et al. 1977) were not read and have no reference records here. Still missing: a larger study of overdose by time since last use with a marker of tolerance; Bird and Hutchinson (2003, Addiction 98, 185-190) and Merrall et al. (2010, doi 10.1111/j.1360-0443.2010.02990.x), cited by the papers read, were not read. Deaths after leaving methadone or buprenorphine treatment (Sordo et al., 2017) and using in an unfamiliar setting (Siegel, 1984) are now separate answers; the naltrexone study White and Irvine describe (Cornish 1993, p. 968) is not claimed here.

evidence_add.extracted: Over 20 months, 137 consecutive people dependent on opiates who were receiving detoxification as part of a 28-day inpatient treatment programme, and who consented to follow-up, were recruited; 5 died within 12 months of discharge, 3 of them after a drug overdose within the first four months; 103 were interviewed at a mean of 8.7 months after discharge, and a records search showed the other 29 alive one year after discharge, so vital status was known for all 137.

evidence_add.locator: Participants, methods, and results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
evidence_add.extracted: To test whether loss of tolerance raised the risk of overdose, the authors grouped people by their presumed opiate tolerance on leaving treatment: 43 'still tolerant' who failed to complete detoxification; 57 'reduced tolerance' who completed the prescribed detoxification but left the programme early; 37 'lost tolerance' who completed detoxification and the whole inpatient programme. The three overdose deaths, all within four months of leaving, were all in the last group; the two deaths not related to overdose, both in people who had relapsed, were one in the 'lost tolerance' group (end-stage renal failure) and one in the 'reduced tolerance' group (Clostridium welchii infection); nobody in the 'still tolerant' group died (Fisher's exact test, df = 2, P = 0.02, without saying whether all deaths or overdose deaths were compared). Mean time to the follow-up interview was 9.5, 8.7 and 7.8 months in the three groups. Editors' calculation (exact binomial 95% intervals): overdose deaths 3 of 37 (8.1%, 1.7% to 21.9%) against 0 of 100 in the two other groups together (0% to 3.6%). No measure of tolerance, or of drug use at or after discharge, is reported.

evidence_add.extracted: From earlier published data, the authors would have expected one or two deaths within a year in a group of this size, and only one from overdose; they call the clustering of overdose deaths among people who completed treatment counterintuitive unless it derives from loss of tolerance and the consequent unpredictability of renewed heroin use, and say the study urgently requires replication. The attribution to lost tolerance is the authors' reading: tolerance was not measured.
